vignette:
Elena has spent the last fifty years building a life of quiet order. As the head librarian at the city’s main branch, she finds a deep, abiding comfort in the hushed aisles, the scent of aging paper, and the unwavering logic of the Dewey Decimal System. It is a world she can control, a universe of knowledge that can be categorized, shelved, and made safe. For decades, this sanctuary has been enough to keep the chaos of the past at bay, relegated to a locked room in the back of her mind.

The key to that room began to turn six months ago. It wasn't a dramatic event, but a mundane one: a construction crew began work on the building across the street from the library. The sudden, percussive bang of a pile driver one morning sent a tremor not just through the floorboards, but through Elena herself. She dropped a stack of books, her hands flying to her ears. In that instant, she was no longer a 78-year-old librarian in a sunlit room in America. She was sixteen again, barefoot on the cold tile of her childhood home, the air thick with the smell of dust and fear. The rhythmic banging wasn't steel on concrete; it was the sound of soldiers’ rifle butts against their neighbor’s front door, a sound that had echoed down their street for a week before it finally arrived at their own.

Since that day, the past is no longer a memory but a constant, intrusive presence. She finds herself scanning the faces of library patrons, a knot of anxiety tightening in her chest when a man in a uniform—a security guard, a mail carrier—walks through the door. A book cart rattling over the grout lines in the floor can make her heart pound with the memory of the truck that took her father away. She has started taking the long way to the circulation desk, avoiding the history section where the deep reds and stark blacks on book covers about political strife seem to scream at her.

Sleep offers little respite. She wakes up two or three times a night, her nightgown damp with sweat, the phantom sensation of her mother’s hand gripping her arm still palpable. Her husband of fifty-two years, Carlos, will stir beside her, murmuring, “¿Estás bien, mi amor?” She always says yes, that it was just a bad dream, because how can she explain that she was dreaming of the frantic, whispered packing in the dark? Of leaving behind her dog, her dolls, the entire geography of her youth, with nothing but a small bag and a terror so profound it felt like it had replaced her bones.

Her relationship with Carlos, once a source of immense comfort, has become strained. He sees her flinch at the evening news, her sudden silences, her new insistence on keeping the curtains drawn after dusk. He knows the broad strokes of her story—the escape, the refugee camp, the long journey—but he knows it as a story that is over, a historical fact of her life that they overcame together. He doesn't understand that for her, it is happening all over again, every day.

She feels a profound sense of detachment from her own life. During Sunday dinners, she watches her grandchildren laugh and argue, and feels as though she is watching them through thick glass. They live in a world of such safety, a world she fought so hard to give them, yet she feels she can never truly join them in it. She carries a secret they will never understand—the knowledge of how quickly a world can be shattered, how the sound of boots on a gravel path can be the end of everything you have ever known. She sits in her comfortable armchair, in the safe and quiet home she built, and waits for the door to be kicked in.
